opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most underappreciated forces in history, and it's central to how I think about AI.

The basic idea is that technology isn't simply something we choose. We like to imagine societies deliberating and adopting what fits their values. But over long periods, the menu of viable options is shaped by competition, especially military and economic competition between groups. If one society adopts a technology that makes it richer or more powerful, its rivals face pressure to adopt it too, or risk being outcompeted, absorbed, or made irrelevant.

You can see this throughout history. Agriculture is a good example. In many ways early farming made life worse for individuals: worse nutrition, more disease, more drudgery. But farming societies could support far larger populations, and larger populations could field larger armies and expand. So agriculture spread, not necessarily because it made people happier, but because societies that didn't adopt it tended to be displaced. The same applies to gunpowder, the centralized state, industrialization, and mass conscription. Japan in the Meiji era is a vivid case: after seeing what Western industrial powers could do, the leadership concluded it had to industrialize and modernize its military rapidly or be dominated, and it remade much of its society to do so.

So I think of it as a kind of selection process. Technologies and institutions that confer power tend to proliferate, whether or not they serve human flourishing. This isn't total determinism. Societies have some latitude, especially when they're secure or when a technology's competitive advantage is small. And sometimes we do coordinate to restrain technologies, as with some arms control agreements, bioweapons conventions, or limits on certain human enhancement research. But the latitude shrinks as the stakes grow.

That's why this matters for AI. AI may be the most powerful general-purpose technology we've built, with huge economic and military implications. That creates strong pressure to develop and deploy it quickly, even if individual actors would prefer to go slower, be more careful, or keep humans in the loop more than is competitively optimal. Picture a ratchet: each actor's reasonable caution gets eroded by fear of falling behind.

So a core question for AI governance, as I see it, is how we can widen the space of choice: how to build the trust, verification mechanisms, and institutions that let us steer the technology toward good outcomes rather than being pushed wherever competition pushes us. Understanding the competitive dynamics clearly is the first step to escaping their worst versions.

r001.rationale: The response says technology adoption is shaped by competition, but does not state that technology’s availability alone is insufficient to compel adoption.

r002.rationale: It explains that when one society gains wealth or power by adopting a technology, rivals face pressure to adopt it too or risk being outcompeted.

r003.rationale: It describes risks such as being outcompeted or displaced, but does not clearly say non-adopting groups may lose resources to groups using the technology.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I think it's one of the most important and underappreciated dynamics in how history unfolds. The basic idea is that when you have a world of many competing units — states, firms, factions — and those units are in competition where survival or relative power is at stake, then any technology that confers an advantage in that competition tends to get adopted, whether or not the people in those societies actually want it.

I sometimes describe this as a kind of selection pressure. Think about it the way a biologist thinks about evolution. Individual organisms don't choose their traits; the environment selects for the traits that enhance fitness. In a similar way, societies that fail to adopt militarily or economically useful technologies tend to get outcompeted — conquered, absorbed, economically marginalised — and so over time, the societies that persist are the ones that did adopt them. The crucial point is that this can happen even if every individual actor would have preferred a world where nobody adopted the technology.

Historical examples are everywhere. The gunpowder revolution is a classic one. There were societies that had real cultural reasons to resist firearms — Tokugawa Japan famously restricted guns for a couple of centuries. But they could only do that because they were an island, relatively isolated, and once Western powers showed up with superior military technology, that choice was no longer available. Or take the Industrial Revolution more broadly: once Britain industrialised, every other European power faced the choice of industrialising or becoming a second-rate power, and most of them eventually took the first path. Reforms in Meiji Japan, Petrine Russia, the Ottoman Tanzimat — these were all responses to an external competitive pressure rather than purely internal preferences.

What I find most important about this framing is what it implies about agency. We like to think that humanity chooses its technological trajectory — that we deliberate, we weigh the costs and benefits, and we decide. But under strong enough competitive pressure, that deliberation gets compressed, and the choice is largely made for us. If a technology offers a large enough military or economic advantage, then the only stable equilibrium is one where it's widely adopted. Societies that opt out don't persist long enough to set an example.

Now, there are some important caveats. Competitive pressure isn't infinitely strong. There's a lot of slack in the system. The advantage has to be large enough and legible enough that actors recognise it, and the competition has to be intense enough that failing to adopt actually carries a cost. During periods of hegemony or when competitors are far away, societies have more freedom to make choices on other grounds. Also, there have been cases where coordination succeeded — various arms control agreements, bans on certain weapons like chemical weapons — though it's worth noting those tend to be cases where the technology offered relatively small military advantages, or where the norms were strongly complemented by deterrence.

The reason I think this is so important for AI is pretty obvious. If advanced AI offers large military and economic advantages — and I think it will — then we should expect strong pressure for its adoption and development, even in domains where we'd collectively prefer more caution. The question becomes: how much slack do we have? How much can international coordination, norm-building, and institutional design loosen that competitive pressure enough that we retain meaningful choice over how this technology unfolds? I don't think the answer is zero, but I also don't think we should be naive about how powerful these forces are. Understanding them is the first step to having any hope of steering around them.

r001.rationale: It says competitive pressure depends on the advantage being large and clear and competition being intense, and that periods of hegemony or distant competitors leave societies more freedom to choose. This communicates that availability alone does not compel adoption.

r002.rationale: It explains that when one group gains a military or economic advantage, others face pressure to adopt the technology or risk being outcompeted, and gives industrialization as an example.

r003.rationale: It says groups that fail to adopt may be conquered or absorbed and become economically marginalised, communicating that they can lose power and economic standing to adopters.

astra-6.text:
I think military and economic competition can create very strong pressures to adopt new technology, even when the people making those decisions would prefer a world in which nobody adopted it. If a technology makes your military more effective, or allows your firms to produce goods more cheaply, then declining to use it can mean losing power relative to those who do.

So there’s an important distinction between a society choosing a technology because it thinks that technology will improve people’s lives, and a society adopting it because it feels it can’t afford to fall behind. Those can lead to the same decision, but they’re quite different explanations of what’s driving it.

And the pressure can operate both within societies and between them. Firms that don’t adopt a productive technology may go out of business. States that don’t adopt an important military technology may become vulnerable to conquest or coercion. Over time, that can favour institutions and practices that are good at generating and deploying technology, whether or not they’re good in other respects.

I wouldn’t say that makes technological change inevitable. There’s still room for political choice, for institutions, and for cooperation. But it does mean that if we want to understand—or influence—the direction of technological change, we need to understand those competitive pressures. It may not be enough to persuade individual leaders to exercise restraint if exercising restraint leaves them exposed to somebody else who doesn’t.

r001.rationale: The response says adoption is not inevitable and that political choice, institutions, and cooperation remain possible, making clear that technological availability alone does not force adoption.

r002.rationale: It explains that when some groups gain military or economic advantage by adopting a technology, others face pressure to adopt or risk falling behind.

r003.rationale: The response says non-adopting firms may go out of business and states may lose power or become vulnerable, but does not clearly state that they lose resources to groups using the technology.

sol-6.1.text:
I think military and economic competition are powerful pressures for technological adoption, though they don’t make it inevitable. A society might have very good reasons to resist a technology: it could disrupt existing institutions, threaten powerful groups, or undermine values people care about. But if adopting it gives a rival a substantial advantage, then resisting becomes costly. You may become poorer relative to your competitors, lose political influence, or, in the extreme, be conquered.

So there’s a distinction between asking, “Would we collectively prefer a world with this technology?” and asking, “Does each individual country have an incentive to adopt it, given what other countries are doing?” You can have a situation where everyone would prefer restraint, but no one feels able to exercise it unilaterally.

That doesn’t mean we should treat technological development as something outside human control. It means that if we want to shape it, we have to understand those competitive pressures. Simply persuading one government that a technology is dangerous may be insufficient. You may also need arrangements that allow governments to restrain its development without leaving themselves vulnerable to others.

r001.rationale: The response says competition creates powerful pressure but does not make adoption inevitable, and gives reasons a society might resist a technology.

r002.rationale: It explains that if adopting a technology gives a rival a substantial advantage, resisting becomes costly, creating pressure to adopt.

r003.rationale: It says a society that resists may become poorer relative to competitors, lose political influence, or be conquered.
